common_name: City Garden Black-Eyed Susan (Compact Container-Friendly Orange Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun to light shade; City Garden is a vegetatively propagated selection, so purchase nursery plants or divisions from an established clump rather than seed for true-to-type, uniformly compact habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to slightly moist soil in full sun to light shade; City Garden is a compact sport of the native orange coneflower (Rudbeckia fulgida) that tops out at about half the height of Goldsturm and similar cultivars, forming a sturdy, upright, rhizome-spreading clump roughly 10-12 inches tall and 16-18 inches wide. From midsummer through early fall it is loaded with the same golden-yellow, dark-brown-coned daisy flowers typical of the species, but on stiff, compact stems that need no staking. Its small stature makes it especially well suited to containers, the front of the border, and small urban or courtyard gardens where full-size black-eyed Susans would overwhelm the space. Like other Rudbeckia fulgida selections it is heat and drought tolerant once established, easy to grow, and attractive to bees, butterflies, and other pollinators through its long bloom season; leaving the seed heads standing into winter also provides food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

common_name: Rustic Dwarfs Black-Eyed Susan (Compact Mahogany-Gold Mixed Rudbeckia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 6-8 weeks early for earlier bloom; press seed onto the soil surface since it needs light to germinate. Rustic Dwarfs is a compact, open-pollinated seed strain, so expect variation in exact color mix from plant to plant.

directions: Rustic Dwarfs (also sold as Rustic Colors) is a compact seed strain of the native black-eyed Susan, reaching only about 14-20 inches tall versus 2-3 feet for the species, making it well suited to containers, edging, and the front of borders where taller Rudbeckia would flop or crowd neighbors. Sturdy, well-branched plants bear abundant single daisy-form flowers up to 5 inches across in a warm mix of rich yellow, gold, bronze, and mahogany tones, often bicolor or zoned, around a prominent dark brown-black central cone. Grow in full sun and average, well-drained soil; plants tolerate heat and short dry spells well once established and bloom heavily from midsummer into autumn. Deadhead to prolong flowering and produce more cut flowers, or allow some heads to mature for self-sowing and reliable return color the following year; the blooms are highly attractive to bees, butterflies, and other pollinators.

common_name: Blue Behemoth Amsonia (Giant Interspecific Blue Star)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; give Blue Behemoth extra room compared to other Amsonia cultivars, since its dome-shaped clumps can eventually reach several feet across.

directions: Blue Behemoth is a patented (PP35930) interspecific hybrid between Amsonia hubrichtii and A. tabernaemontana, selected by Chicagoland Grows for its dramatically larger scale, reaching roughly 40-42 inches tall and spreading up to 8 feet wide at maturity, several times the footprint of most other blue star cultivars. In spring it produces an extended, heavy show of narrow-petaled, very pale icy-blue star-shaped flowers on an upright, dome-shaped, shrub-like clump of long, narrow, dark green leaves that need no staking. Like other Amsonia, it is untroubled by deer, rabbits, pests, or disease once established, tolerates heat and drought, and turns a glowing pale golden yellow in autumn, with the sturdy stems persisting through much of winter for added season-long structure. Its large size makes it best suited to borders, foundation plantings, and naturalized or matrix plantings with room to spread, rather than small garden beds.
